obtained.how: institutional repository copy: VTechWorks (Virginia Tech) electronic thesis, open bitstream (147-page PDF with a text layer)

bibliography.note: Author is Johnathan Lee Harris ("Harris, J. L." would be fuller); MS in Fisheries and Wildlife Sciences, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Blacksburg, approved April 28, 2006; title agrees

claims.claim: small (< 100 mm) white perch in the reservoir were collected (found) only in unvegetated littoral areas — used as evidence of habitat use relative to plant beds
claims.source_value: the words are there, but only unvegetated shorelines were sampled (age-0 fish by "seining shallow, unvegetated shorelines", then shoreline electrofishing), in a reservoir whose ~5-m annual water-level swing limits the establishment of significant aquatic vegetation. The sentence (in the crappie-diet discussion) contrasts the inshore small perch with offshore adult crappies; it says nothing about avoidance of plants
claims.location: p. 104 (PDF p. 116); sampling p. 26 (PDF p. 38) and p. 63 (PDF p. 75); vegetation p. 11 (PDF p. 23)
claims.quote: white perch were only collected in unvegetated, littoral areas where adult crappies were not present
claims.conditions: Kerr Reservoir (19,790 ha, VA–NC), upper end; June–November 2004–2005; seine and boat electrofishing along unvegetated shorelines; little aquatic vegetation in the reservoir
claims.note: Drop it as evidence about plant beds (§3.4.8) and about habitat choice (§3.7.8), or state that only unvegetated shores were sampled in a nearly plant-free reservoir

claims.claim: young white perch moved shallow after dark (Harris 2006)
claims.source_value: a general, uncited sampling rationale for all age-0 fishes: "all age-0 collection took place after dark, the period when most age-0 fish migrate to shallow areas"; no day–night comparison or white perch observation
claims.quote: after dark, the period when most age-0 fish migrate to shallow areas
claims.note: not evidence of a white perch diel movement

claims.claim: white perch growth slowed as numbers rose in an invaded reservoir
claims.quote: Mean length of age-1 white perch declined from 124 mm TL in 1995 to 101
claims.conditions: Kerr Reservoir; age-1 mean TL 124 mm (1995) → 101 mm (2005); age-2 159 mm (1995) → 142 mm (2004); Harris reads it as density-dependent growth "in years after they became abundant"
claims.note: Harris adds that the population had not become "severely stunted" (p. 91), reaching 230 mm TL by age 3

claims.claim: in Kerr Reservoir, where shad were available, white perch were under 2 % by weight of every sportfish diet
claims.source_value: < 2 % by weight for every sportfish species in both years EXCEPT walleye in 2004, when a single white perch made up 17 % of walleye stomach contents by weight (7 walleye with food; Harris treats it with caution). White perch were found in only 4 of 1,172 adult piscivores collected (1 largemouth, 1 striped bass and 1 walleye in 2004; 1 striped bass in 2005)
claims.location: p. iii (PDF p. 3), Abstract; p. 85–86 (PDF p. 97–98), Results; p. 104 (PDF p. 116)
claims.quote: exceeded 2% of diet by weight for any sportfish species in either year, excluding walleye
claims.conditions: adult catfishes, crappies, largemouth, striped bass, walleye and white bass; 387 fish in 2004 and 785 in 2005, mostly from fall gill nets; clupeids (threadfin and gizzard shad) were the main fish prey of every species
claims.note: the abstract's summary is "low (< 2% of diets by weight)"; write "under 2 % by weight of every sportfish diet but one small walleye sample"

claims.claim: young white perch shift to amphipods and chironomids from ~40 mm (Prout, Mills & Forney 1990, via Harris 2006)
claims.quote: diet shift at 40 mm TL (from copepods and daphnids to amphipods and chironomids)
claims.conditions: age-0 white perch, Oneida Lake, New York (Prout et al. 1990); 40 mm TL
claims.note: Harris also cites a shift at 40 mm TL in the James River (copepods and Leptodora → mysids, insect larvae and pupae; Rudershausen & Loesch 2000) and at 50 mm TL in the Richibucto Estuary (St-Hilaire et al. 2002)

notes: The main correction: Harris's "only collected in unvegetated, littoral areas" is a sampling artefact (only unvegetated shores were sampled, in a reservoir with little vegetation), so it should not appear as evidence about plant beds (§3.4.8) or about where young white perch live (§3.7.8). The "moved shallow after dark" is a methods rationale, not a finding. Other useful values: white perch were ovivorous in the Roanoke River in May (striped bass egg occurrence up to 100 % of perch at times) but modelled consumption was small; adult white perch overlapped strongly with adult crappie (> 0.6); white perch eaten by predators were 82–152 mm TL (mean 110); white bass declined after the white perch invasion.
